concepts.def: Selecting food based on accurate information such as labels, prices and nutritional content rather than on advertising alone.
The legal protections shoppers have, such as the right to refunds for faulty or misdescribed food under consumer protection law.
Showing the price per standard measure, such as per 100g or per litre, so consumers can compare products of different sizes fairly.
The mandatory packaging information, including ingredients, allergens and date marks, that enables consumers to choose safely and wisely.
Promotions such as buy-one-get-one-free or multibuys that can save money but may also encourage over-buying and food waste.
Planning shopping around a set amount of money, comparing prices and avoiding waste to make food spending go further.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Being an Effective Consumer of Food — a core area of GCSE Food Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Being an Effective Consumer of Food brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Being an Effective Consumer of Food.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: 'Buy one get one free' promotions can cause problems because they may encourage:
options: Over-buying and food waste
Better nutrition
Allergen labelling
Longer shelf life

mcqs.q: Unit pricing helps consumers by showing the:
options: Price per standard measure
Brand's history
Advertising budget
Delivery cost

mcqs.q: If food is faulty or misdescribed, consumers have a right to a:
options: Refund
Free advert
Tax rebate
Loyalty card

mcqs.q: Making an 'informed choice' about food means relying mainly on:
options: Accurate label and price information
Television adverts
Packaging colour
Brand fame

mcqs.q: Are 'buy one get one free' offers always good value?
options: They are illegal in supermarkets.
They are always the cheapest choice with no downsides.
The right to free items for life.
Not always; they can encourage buying more than needed, leading to waste.

mcqs.q: What does unit pricing allow a shopper to do?
options: See only the brand's recommended retail price.
The right to free items for life.
Compare the price per standard measure across different pack sizes.
Find out the food's calorie content.

mcqs.q: If a food product is faulty, what right does a consumer have?
options: No right at all once the item has left the shop.
The right to a refund, repair or replacement under consumer law.
They are illegal in supermarkets.
The right to free items for life.
